claims.text: Japanese set-meal kitchen using soy sauce, dashi, and wheat-containing dishes (croquettes, hamburgers); no gluten-free protocol documented.
Standard Japanese seasonings including soy sauce are used; soy sauce typically contains wheat and no wheat-free alternative is mentioned.
Fish dashi/stock is used in cooking and meat/fish mains are on the menu, so vegan and vegetarian dishes share a non-vegan kitchen.
The owner asks customers to communicate dietary concerns and allergies in advance when reserving by email.
Cooking is centered on seasonal vegetables, with a course featuring around ten seasonal vegetable dishes.

name: グリル・チェンバー (Grill Chamber)

claims.text: Menu is wheat-centric: demi-glace sauce (wheat-roux based) tops the signature rice dish, and mains include breaded chicken cutlet and hamburg steak — high gluten exposure with no documented gluten-free handling.
Core dishes are built on meat, egg, sausage and meat-based demi-glace; no vegan or vegetarian preparations are documented.
Udon (wheat noodles) are a core part of the lunch menu and are prepared in the same small kitchen, creating gluten cross-contact risk.
Standard sushi-style soy sauce (made with wheat) is used throughout, as is typical for a traditional sushi-ya; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.
All dishes are built around fish/seafood and fish dashi; even the chirashi's tofu is served over and alongside fish, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.

name: 発酵薬膳料理 らふぁえろ (Hakko Yakuzen Ryori Raffaello)

claims.text: The signature fermented set meal is described as including grilled fish as a main alongside the vegetable dishes, with no vegan/vegetarian distinction noted, so plant-based diners cannot assume the standard meal is fish-free.

Cooking relies on fermented, pesticide-free vegetables and a house fermentation water, with the kitchen stating it uses almost no conventional seasoning and serves very lightly seasoned, vegetable-forward food.
Set meals include tempura (wheat batter) and the Asuka hotpot is traditionally finished with udon (wheat), indicating wheat is used throughout the kitchen.
Traditional Yamato cuisine here uses soy sauce (usukuchi/light soy in the hotpot), which normally contains wheat.
Core dishes use chicken broth, milk, fish dashi, eggs and the dairy-based 蘇 (su); no vegan menu is documented.
This is a flour-based bakery where every product is made with domestic wheat, so there is pervasive wheat/gluten throughout the kitchen and no gluten-free options exist.
Documented breads include dairy and egg items (milk-style shokupan, almond melon pan, anko-and-butter), so animal ingredients and shared surfaces are common; no vegan-specific handling is described.
The bakery emphasizes domestic wheat and local Nara ingredients (Nara rice, Yamato tea), so ingredient sourcing is transparent and locally focused.
Menu is dominated by wheat noodles (udon, sara-udon) and breaded/fried tonkatsu and katsudon, so shared cooking surfaces and fryers make cross-contact effectively unavoidable.
Broth and donburi dishes are seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, and rely on fish dashi.
Dishes are built around beef, chicken, pork, and egg with fish/meat broths; no plant-only options are documented.
The signature dishes are built on dairy-based milk and yogurt espuma foams, so the core menu is not dairy-free.
As a shaved-ice shop, the base is simply ice with fruit syrups, so a non-dairy fruit version may be possible if requested, though this is not documented.
